whyThisMatters: If you can name the trick out loud together, you will spot it faster on your own — whether you are at your desk or on the bridge with limited time.
rememberThis: If you can name the trick, you can spot it next time. Put a word to what felt strange — then STOP, VERIFY through a channel you already trust, and REPORT.

discussionPrompts: Ask someone to explain one of these terms in their own words before you show the answer. Could they explain it to a colleague who missed today, without using jargon?

Ask which two terms are easiest to mix up and why. The fake link (the address shown in an email) and the fake portal (the whole login page being copied) are the most confused — both involve a wrong destination, but they are different checks.
Ask for a real example from their own inbox or phone that matches one of these terms — for example, a crewing email with an extra word in the address.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often mix up FAKE LINK and FAKE PORTAL. Both involve a wrong destination, so people pick one when the riddle points to the other. The difference: a fake link is the clickable address inside a message; a fake portal is the entire login page that looks real but sits at a fake address.

riddles.riddle: You get an email that looks like it is from Crewing — hr@synergymarine-group-careers.com. But your real Crewing address is hr@synergymarinegroup.com. I just added one extra word with a hyphen. What trick am I?
I am a message that says "ACT NOW or your allotment will be delayed!" and "Do not call your vessel manager — just click here!" I want you to hurry so you do not stop and check. What trick am I?
You think I am your crew payslip as a PDF. But my file name ends with .pdf.exe — the last part is .exe, not .pdf. I also ask you to click "Enable Content" to see me. What trick am I?

In your rotation email you see the crew portal address portal.synergymarinegroup.com written in blue. But when you press and hold the link (or hover on a computer), it actually goes to a different place with "-secure" in the name. What trick am I?

I look exactly like the real crew portal login page where you check your rotation and payslips. But my address at the top has one extra letter — synergymanne instead of synergymarine. What trick am I?

I am a fake text message (SMS) on your phone. I say "Your crew rotation portal link has changed — tap here to confirm your sign-off dates for MV Horizon." I use a short link like bit.ly to hide where I really go. What trick am I?

A small box pops up on your screen and says "Type your password here to fix the error." Whether you are at your desk or on a shared computer on board, the real IT support team never asks for your password this way. What trick am I?
I send your phone many "Approve this login?" messages — the second check after your password — again and again. I hope you get tired and tap Approve just to make me stop. What trick am I?
I am the three-step habit: 1. STOP before you act, 2. VERIFY using a number or portal you already trust, 3. REPORT to the IT support team. What is this rule called?
